shipped.warum: The record of the sessions, from Quicherat's edition (1841), read against the page images, in Latin and in the surviving French minute, with Murray's English (1902) or a working translation: the oath, 'Jeannette', the voice in her father's garden, 'if I am not, may God put me there', the English to lose everything in France, God and the Church 'all one', the standard 'in the labour' and 'in the honour', and her own account of the death of Franquet d'Arras.

shipped.kurz: The Twelve Articles and the University of Paris
shipped.warum: From Quicherat's edition (1841), read against the page images, with a working translation: the promoter's list of what she should be declared, three of the Twelve Articles about 'a certain woman' (the voices and the fairies' tree, the dress of a man, no man in the world but God), and the verdicts of the doctors at Rouen and of the faculties of theology and decrees of Paris: 'Belial, Satan and Behemoth', schism and apostasy.

shipped.kurz: Saint-Ouen: abjuration, relapse and sentence (24–30 May 1431)
shipped.warum: From Quicherat's edition (1841), read against the page images, in the French minute and the Latin record with a working translation: her appeal to the pope refused at Saint-Ouen, the abjuration signed with a mark, perpetual prison 'with the bread of sorrow', the women's clothes, the relapse of 28 May ('for fear of the fire'), and the sentence of 30 May: 'as a rotten limb'.

From Quicherat's fifth volume (1849), read against the page images, with a working translation: the summons to the English before Orléans ('I am a chief of war'), the plea to the duke of Burgundy on the coronation day, her discontent with the truces in a letter to Reims, a request for powder and saltpetre to Riom with her signature, and the threatening letter to the Hussites of Bohemia, in the German version Quicherat printed.

shipped.kurz: The Journal of the siege of Orléans (March–May 1429)
shipped.warum: The city's own book, put together about 1467 from a register kept during the siege, from Quicherat's fourth volume (1847), read against the page images, with a working translation: the English answer to her letter ('whore', 'cowgirl', the threat of fire), her entry by torchlight 'as if they saw God come down among them', the Bastard's threat to kill the prisoners, the arrow at the Tourelles and 'En nom de Dieu', the bridge that 'gave way' (Quicherat: it was burned on purpose), and the Sunday on which she forbade the French to attack.

shipped.kurz: Christine de Pizan, Ditié de Jehanne d'Arc (31 July 1429)
shipped.warum: The only French verse written in her lifetime that has come down to us, by the author of the City of Ladies, a fortnight after Reims; twenty stanzas from Quicherat's fifth volume (1849), read against the page images, with a line-for-line working translation: 'Johanne, de bonne heure née', 'what honour to the female sex', the English dead in the furrows, the heretics she will destroy, the Holy Land where she is to die, and the threat to Paris.

shipped.kurz: The Burgundian chronicler: Monstrelet on the Maid (1429–1430)
shipped.warum: Enguerrand de Monstrelet, Jean de Luxembourg's chronicler, from Quicherat's fourth volume (1847), read against the page images, with a working translation: the servant from an inn whom the king's council 'held for a madwoman', the beheading of Franquet d'Arras, the capture before Compiègne, and the duke of Burgundy's words to her, which Monstrelet heard and 'did not well remember'. What he leaves out, the sale to the English, is named in the notes.

shipped.kurz: The witnesses of the nullity trial (1456)
shipped.warum: Six depositions from Quicherat's second and third volumes (1844–1845), read against the page images, in the Latin of the record with a working translation: her friend Hauviette on the fairies' tree and her tears, Jean de Metz on Vaucouleurs ('even if I wear my feet down to the knees'), Dunois on 'En nom Dieu' and the wind on the Loire, Marguerite La Touroulde on the rosaries, the notary Manchon on the English secretaries and the bishop's 'fine trial', and the usher Massieu on the schedule of 'about eight lines'.

shipped.kurz: The end, as two friars remembered it (1450)
shipped.warum: Isambart de la Pierre and Martin Ladvenu before the first royal inquiry of March 1450, from Quicherat's second volume (1844), read against the page images, in French with a working translation: the appeal to the council of Basel kept out of the record, 'Farowelle, it is done', 'I die through you', the secular judge who never passed sentence, the cross from the nearest church, and the executioner's fear. The burning itself is not described.

The sentence of the papal judges at Rouen, from Quicherat's third volume (1845), read against the page images, in Latin with a working translation: the suit of her mother and brothers, the refusal to judge her revelations ('more worthy of admiration than of condemnation'), the Twelve Articles torn up as 'corruptly, deceitfully, slanderously' extracted, the trial, the abjuration and the sentences declared 'null, invalid, void and empty', and a cross for the Old Market.

missing.warum: The friars of 1450 and 1456, the Journal of a Parisian bourgeois and several chroniclers describe her death in detail, and what the executioner said afterwards. This site carries her words, the procedure and the men who carried it out, and the sentence's own phrase, 'cruel and horrible burning'; it does not carry the descriptions. Where an excerpt reaches one, the cut is marked and explained. Not carried by choice.
missing.quelle: Quicherat II, pp. 6–7, and III; Quicherat IV (chronicles).

missing.kurz: The English government's letter on her death (June 1431)
missing.warum: The letters in the name of Henry VI to the emperor, the kings and princes of Christendom and to the prelates of France, justifying the sentence, survive and are printed by Quicherat; Monstrelet copies one in place of an account of the trial. The court's own sentence is carried instead (Ouen Sentence [1]). Not carried by choice; a candidate for a later stage.
missing.quelle: Quicherat I (1841), pp. 485–492; Monstrelet in Quicherat IV.

missing.warum: Jean Gerson's short treatise on the Maid (14 May 1429), probably his last writing, and the opinions written for the nullity trial argue the case at length; the sentence of nullity cites them as its grounds. They are long, learned and mostly untranslated. Not carried in stage 1; the first candidates for a second stage.

Perceval de Cagny, Jean Chartier, the herald Berry and others follow her from Patay to Paris and Compiègne. Stage 1 carries the city of Orléans' Journal and the Burgundian Monstrelet, one for each side; the rest are left for a later stage. Not carried in stage 1.

missing.kurz: Modern translations of the whole record
missing.warum: The complete English translation of the trial of condemnation by W. P. Barrett (1931) and the French of the later editions are, or may still be, in copyright. This site uses T. Douglas Murray's English of 1902 where it was checked against the Latin, and its own working translation elsewhere. A gap by necessity.
missing.quelle: W. P. Barrett, The Trial of Jeanne d'Arc (London 1931), in copyright.
